Let

\[
s_r(Q)=Q_1^r+Q_2^r+Q_3^r.
\]

The conditions are

\[
\mathbb E s_2=\frac12,\qquad \mathbb E s_3=\frac{11}{36},
\]

and we need the range of \(\mathbb E s_5\).

Sharp cubic bounds on \(x^5\), summed over \(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3\), give

\[
\frac{19}{144}\le \mathbb E s_5\le \frac{251}{1296}.
\]

For the lower bound, equality forces every coordinate of \(Q\) to be either \(1/6\) or \(2/3\), hence

\[
Q \text{ is a permutation of } \left(\frac23,\frac16,\frac16\right)
\]

almost surely. Therefore \(K=3\) almost surely at the lower endpoint.

For the upper bound, equality forces \(Q\) almost surely to be one of the following types:

\[
(1,0,0),\qquad \left(\frac12,\frac12,0\right),\qquad \left(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13\right),
\]

up to permutation. If their total probabilities by support size are \(p_1,p_2,p_3\), then the constraints give

\[
\frac{p_3}{27}=\frac1{54}\implies p_3=\frac12,
\]

and

\[
\frac{p_2}{4}+\frac{p_3}{3}=\frac14\implies p_2=\frac13,
\]

so

\[
p_1=1-\frac13-\frac12=\frac16.
\]

Since both endpoints are attainable and the feasible laws are convex, every intermediate value is attainable.

\[
\boxed{\left(\left[\frac{19}{144},\frac{251}{1296}\right],\,3,\,\left(\frac16,\frac13,\frac12\right)\right)}
\]
